<reason>Both sides were sharp, but PRO (B) built the cleaner path. Its "remember vs honor" frame, the argument that a plaque cannot outvote a pedestal, and the turn on CON's "names carved at the base" proposal (staging the hierarchy permanently) survived the whole debate. CON's best line—criterion instability (Washington vs Lee, Colston vs the "primarily" test)—landed real hits, but PRO's "what the honor rests on" answer stayed coherent and PRO showed CON's remedies require the same judgment. CON's Rebuttal 2 pivot ("I do not commit to Colston back on his plinth") effectively conceded that removal was right in PRO's flagship case, shifting CON from "annotate, don't remove" to "decide case by case," which blunted its own remedy. PRO's reversibility reversal (object intact and re-erectable vs. chiseled names) and asymmetric-cost weighing (dead man's reputation vs. the living child) gave the judge a clean decision rule. CON also lost two turns to clipping, including the key "frame is whatever the city says" point, which PRO's closing then dismantled.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's dilemma (Q2: either context defeats form so the annotated square works, or the museum is theatre) was PRO's biggest threat; PRO's A2 answered it directly—the museum speaks in the voice of evidence, the building already withdrew the claim, "nobody sees a Klan robe in a vitrine and concludes endorsement"—and the closing sealed it by showing the square's frame is the plinth and maintenance budget, not the city's words.</best_rebuttal>
